template.name: Functional Equation Classification via Special Values and Structural Induction
template.description: A strategy for determining all feasible values of an integer-valued function at a fixed argument when the function class is defined by global conditions (such as nested subscript identities or inequalities involving function composition). The method proceeds by substituting special values to extract constraints, proving that any solution must possess a simple structure (e.g., monotonicity, linear upper bounds, at most one exceptional index), classifying all solutions into 'trivial branch + a few special branches', and substituting each class back for verification. Common pitfalls include incomplete classification (missing special solutions), proving only necessity without sufficiency, and ignoring boundary conditions imposed by the codomain (positive integers vs. non-negative integers). For iterative equations, first prove a_n ≥ n+1, then define the difference b_p = a_p − (p+1) ≥ 0 to simplify. Solutions are classified into the 'trivial branch' and the 'special index branch'; both must be listed to obtain the complete set of possible values (double-value set). For range-characterization problems: prove monotonicity and an upper bound C(n) ≤ n+1, then for each k construct the piecewise function C_k(n) = max(1, n − N + k), yielding the full range {1, …, N+1}—note the upper endpoint is N+1, not N (the extremal construction C(n) = n+1 is valid). When finding all possible values, the special index branch must be searched out (e.g., by brute-force backtracking for the truncated version n ≤ 30); reporting only the trivial branch counts as missing solutions.
applicability: Integer-valued functions defined by nested subscript identities or inequalities with function composition
Problems asking for all feasible values of the function at a fixed argument
Range-characterization problems where monotonicity and linear upper bounds can be established
Truncated finite cases (e.g., n ≤ 30) where special branches can be found by brute-force backtracking

steps.step: Substitute special values to extract initial constraints
steps.detail: Set some variables to specific values (e.g., 0, 1, or boundary values) in the given functional equation or inequality to obtain concrete relations and bounds. Pay attention to the codomain (positive integers or non-negative integers) to avoid invalid boundary cases.

steps.step: Prove structural properties of arbitrary solutions
steps.detail: Use induction or iterative reasoning to establish that any solution must have a simple structure: monotonicity, a linear upper bound (e.g., C(n) ≤ n+1), or at most one exceptional index. For iterative equations, first prove a_n ≥ n+1, then introduce b_p = a_p − (p+1) ≥ 0 to simplify the recurrence.

steps.step: Classify all candidate solutions into branches
steps.detail: Divide solutions into the 'trivial branch' (e.g., a_n = n+1 or C(n) = n+1) and the 'special index branch' (where one or a few indices deviate from the trivial pattern). Ensure the classification is complete; missing special solutions is a common error.

steps.step: Construct explicit solutions for each candidate value
steps.detail: For each candidate value at the fixed argument, explicitly construct a function satisfying the original condition. For range-characterization, for each k construct C_k(n) = max(1, n − N + k) to show the range is exactly {1, …, N+1}. Verify that the upper endpoint N+1 is attainable via C(n) = n+1.

steps.step: Verify sufficiency and compile the complete value set
steps.detail: Substitute each branch back into the original condition to confirm sufficiency (not just necessity). For finite truncated cases (e.g., n ≤ 30), use brute-force backtracking to search the special index branch. The final set of possible values must include contributions from both branches; reporting only the trivial branch is incomplete.

template.name: Residue Class Clustering and Pigeonhole Extremal Bounds
template.description: A strategy for approximation and clustering extremal problems on integer arrays. Objects are classified by residue classes modulo a chosen number (prefix-sum residue classes, multiple classes, or coprime classes). The pigeonhole principle is applied to guarantee that some residue class accumulates sufficiently many elements, yielding the required structure: either proving the existence of a subset sum falling within a given interval, or proving the non-existence of three pairwise coprime elements. Explicit constructions are then used to prove the tightness of the bounds. Key route: select a modulus related to the target value's special residue structure; the union of multiples of 2 or 3 is the standard construction for handling coprime constraints; subset sums are expressed as differences of prefix sums. Warnings: improper modulus choice leads to weak pigeonhole conclusions; coprime problems often omit supplementary discussion of elements coprime to both 2 and 3; interval endpoint inclusion errors must be avoided.
applicability: Subset-sum approximation problems requiring existence proofs via residue-class clustering
Extremal problems forbidding pairwise coprime triples in integer sets
Problems where bounds must be proved tight by explicit constructions (e.g., unions of arithmetic progressions)
Calibration of closed-form parameters using small-scale enumeration

steps.step: Choose modulus and define residue classes
steps.detail: Select a modulus d related to the target value or interval structure. Partition the relevant objects (e.g., prefix sums S_0, S_1, ..., S_n, or array elements) into residue classes modulo d. For subset-sum problems, work with the n+1 prefix sums S_i = sum_{j=1}^i a_j (with S_0 = 0).

steps.step: Apply pigeonhole principle to obtain a collision or dense class
steps.detail: For subset-sum upper bounds: place the n+1 prefix sums into d residue classes. If n+1 > d, two prefix sums fall in the same class, so their difference (a contiguous subset sum) is divisible by d. Combine with element upper-bound estimates to force the subset sum into the target interval. For coprime problems: classify elements by their residue/prime-divisibility structure to show that any sufficiently large set must contain a forbidden configuration or, conversely, to bound the size of a set avoiding it.

steps.step: Construct extremal examples to prove tightness
steps.detail: For pairwise-coprime triple avoidance, the standard maximal construction is the union of multiples of 2 and multiples of 3 within [1, a+2] (or the relevant range). The count is given by inclusion-exclusion: floor((a+2)/2) + floor((a+2)/3) - floor((a+2)/6). For subset-sum lower bounds, construct a mixed sequence containing a few (m-1)-type values and many m-type values to create a precise gap to the nearest achievable subset sum.

steps.step: Calibrate parameters and verify two-sided closure
steps.detail: For subset-sum approximation, the upper and lower bounds must form a closed two-sided loop: the upper bound comes from the pigeonhole collision on n+1 prefix sums modulo d together with element magnitude estimates; the lower bound comes from the explicit mixed-sequence construction. The final modulus d is chosen at the two-sided closure point, calibrated by small-scale enumeration. Do not guess d from one-sided analysis alone.

steps.step: Check endpoint inclusion and coprime-to-6 elements
steps.detail: Verify whether interval endpoints are included or excluded in the target subset-sum range. In coprime extremal problems, explicitly account for elements that are coprime to both 2 and 3 (i.e., coprime to 6); omitting this supplementary discussion is a common error that invalidates the bound.

template.name: Sorted Triple Pairing Triangle Preservation
template.description: After arranging each group of triple side lengths in descending order and pairing them position-wise, the paired triple still forms a triangle. This is proved using the original group's triangle inequality and the monotonicity of sorting: any side is less than the sum of the other two sides in its original group, and those other two sides are no larger than the corresponding sides in the paired triple. This argument implies that the head of the paired sequence must be legal. The solution route first proves the first pair is always legal, concluding that illegal positions can only appear at the tail; then uses an extreme construction where the entire tail is illegal to prove the bound is attainable. Common pitfalls: mismatch between descending order direction and inequality direction; failing to ensure all original group triangle inequalities hold while constructing an illegal tail.
applicability: Applicable to problems involving pairing elements from multiple triples of side lengths while preserving the triangle inequality
Applicable when analyzing the structure of legal/illegal positions in sorted paired sequences of triples
Applicable for constructing extremal examples to show bounds are attainable under triangle inequality constraints

steps.step: Sort each triple of side lengths in descending order
steps.detail: For each group of three side lengths, arrange them as a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ a_3, b_1 ≥ b_2 ≥ b_3, etc. Ensure the descending order is strictly maintained so that inequality directions align correctly in subsequent steps.

steps.step: Pair the sorted triples position-wise
steps.detail: Form a new triple by taking the i-th largest elements from each sorted group. For example, pairing the largest elements together, the second largest together, and the smallest together to form (a_1, b_1, c_1), (a_2, b_2, c_2), (a_3, b_3, c_3).

steps.step: Prove the first paired triple is always legal (forms a triangle)
steps.detail: For the first paired triple (a_1, b_1, c_1), assume without loss of generality that a_1 is the largest. Since the original group of a_1 satisfies the triangle inequality, a_1 < a_2 + a_3. By sorting monotonicity, a_2 ≤ b_1 and a_3 ≤ c_1 (or corresponding paired elements), so a_1 < b_1 + c_1. Thus the first paired triple satisfies the triangle inequality and is legal.

steps.step: Conclude illegal positions can only appear at the tail
steps.detail: Since the head (first paired triple) is proven always legal, any violation of the triangle inequality in the paired sequence must occur at later positions (the tail). This structural conclusion restricts where invalid configurations can arise.

steps.step: Construct an extreme case to show the tail bound is attainable
steps.detail: Design an explicit construction where all tail positions are illegal while ensuring every original group still satisfies the triangle inequality. This demonstrates that the theoretical bound on the number of illegal positions is tight and achievable. Care must be taken to verify all original group triangle inequalities hold in this construction.

template.name: Column-block decomposition and state-transition matrix for Hamiltonian path counting on narrow rectangular grids
template.description: For counting Hamiltonian paths on small-size rectangular grids under specified edge-movement rules (adjacent within the same row or round-trip jumps between columns), decompose the path by the number of visited cycles/column visit blocks: the points in each column are partitioned into several consecutive interval blocks, where the number of blocks corresponds to the number of cycles. Then characterize the legal concatenation between adjacent column blocks using a state-transition matrix (incorporating parity of the block-height sequence and endpoint constraints), accumulating column by column via matrix multiplication. Finally, account for starting-point symmetry. First enumerate the number of cycles, and use the height of the column containing the endpoint together with parity constraints to rule out infeasible cycle counts; set up recurrences separately for feasible cycle counts and sum them; do not forget to multiply by the starting-column symmetry factor. Common pitfalls include omitting the restriction the endpoint column imposes on the number of cycles, confusing the intra-block visit order with inter-block transitions, and mishandling boundary conditions of the block-height sequence (such as fixed heights in the first and last columns). For the 3-row × m-column cylindrical/annulus case: first calibrate on small scales m = 2, 4, 6 (example values 2, 12, 42), fit a closed form of the type m·(2^{m/2} − 1), then substitute back into the problem scale to report the numerical value (the answer is an integer on the order of ten thousands; do not report intermediate lemmas classified by row parity). Full-scale (≥ 60 vertices) brute-force DFS is infeasible within the time limit; the program must extrapolate after small-scale fitting and actually call the main function to print the result. Do not assume a structure first and then self-prove it.
applicability: Counting Hamiltonian paths on small-size rectangular grids under same-row adjacent or inter-column round-trip jump movement rules
Problems where the path can be decomposed by number of cycles / column visit blocks with consecutive interval blocks per column
3-row × m-column cylindrical/annulus instances where small-scale calibration values at m = 2, 4, 6 are 2, 12, 42 and a closed form of type m·(2^{m/2} − 1) is fitted
Instances with ≥ 60 vertices where brute-force DFS is infeasible within the time limit, requiring small-scale fitting and extrapolation

steps.step: Decompose the path by number of cycles / column visit blocks
steps.detail: Partition the points of each column into several consecutive interval blocks; the number of blocks corresponds to the number of cycles. This decomposition is the basis for subsequent state-transfer modeling.

steps.step: Model legal concatenation between adjacent column blocks with a state-transition matrix
steps.detail: Use a state-transition matrix to encode legal transitions between adjacent column blocks, incorporating constraints from the parity of the block-height sequence and endpoint constraints. Accumulate column by column via matrix multiplication.

steps.step: Enumerate cycle counts and prune infeasible ones using endpoint-column height and parity
steps.detail: First enumerate the number of cycles. Use the height of the column containing the endpoint together with parity constraints to exclude infeasible cycle counts. Set up recurrences separately for each feasible cycle count and sum the results.

steps.step: Apply starting-column symmetry factor
steps.detail: After summing over feasible cycle counts, multiply by the starting-column symmetry factor (the number of columns) to account for starting-point symmetry.

steps.step: Calibrate with small-scale state-compression DP before branching by cycle count
steps.detail: First use small-scale state-compression DP for exact enumeration to calibrate. Then branch by cycle count: infeasible cycle counts are excluded by endpoint-column height and parity. Counts in each branch often take the form of a sum of a power of 2 and one less than a power of 2 (2^k + (2^k − 1) type). Finally multiply by the starting-column symmetry factor (number of columns).

steps.step: Handle the 3-row × m-column cylindrical/annulus case via small-scale fitting and closed-form extrapolation
steps.detail: For the 3-row × m-column cylindrical/annulus case, first calibrate on small scales m = 2, 4, 6 with example values 2, 12, 42. Fit a closed form of the type m·(2^{m/2} − 1), then substitute back into the problem scale to report the numerical value. The answer is an integer on the order of ten thousands; do not report intermediate lemmas classified by row parity.

steps.step: Avoid brute-force DFS for full-scale instances and do not assume structure before proof
steps.detail: For full-scale instances (≥ 60 vertices), brute-force DFS is infeasible within the time limit. The program must extrapolate after small-scale fitting and actually call the main function to print the result. Do not assume a structure first and then self-prove it.

template.name: Frequency vector fixed points and 2-cycles for polynomial product identities
template.description: A polynomial product identity can be translated into the statement that the frequency vectors of roots are mutual multiplicity vectors of each other, i.e., a fixed point of the self-composition of the frequency mapping. The frequency mapping acting on integer partitions yields the conjugate partition; its fixed points (self-conjugate partitions) and 2-cycles together give the complete solution structure, from which the attainable values of the target weighted sum are computed. Warning: missing the paired 2-cycle class, writing the conjugate partition shape incorrectly, or mismatching the weighted sum with the partition structure will all lead to errors. Both branches must be searched.
applicability: Problems where a polynomial product identity is equivalent to a root-multiplicity frequency vector equation
Cases where the frequency mapping equals partition conjugation, so solutions are fixed points (self-conjugate) or 2-cycles
Computing attainable values of a target weighted sum based on the partition structure

steps.step: Rewrite the polynomial identity as a frequency vector equation system
steps.detail: Translate the given polynomial product identity into equations relating the frequencies (multiplicities) of each root. Let the frequency vector record how many times each multiplicity occurs.

steps.step: Identify the frequency mapping as partition conjugation
steps.detail: Recognize that the frequency mapping F acting on the integer partition of root multiplicities is exactly the conjugate partition operation. Thus F maps a partition to its conjugate.

steps.step: Classify solutions into self-conjugate fixed points and paired 2-cycles
steps.detail: The condition requires a to be a periodic point of F² (F = frequency/conjugate mapping). The solution set equals fixed points (self-conjugate partitions) union 2-cycles. Both branches must be enumerated; reporting only one branch loses points.

steps.step: Describe the self-conjugate branch shape
steps.detail: The self-conjugate branch has the form a₁ = n−4, a₂ = 2, a₃ = 1, a_{n−4} = 1. There are two additional distinct groups in the 2-cycle branch.

steps.step: Compute the target weighted value for each branch and collect into a set
steps.detail: According to the problem statement, list the target value for each branch completely and answer as a set. Ensure the weighted calculation corresponds correctly to the partition structure.

template.name: Periodic DP and Draw Conditions in Perfect-Information Take-Number Games
template.description: Perfect-information placement/take-number games can be solved via state-space dynamic programming to compute minimax values. Results often exhibit modular periodicity: each full period contributes a fixed amount, and the remainder is looked up in a small table. Alternatively, for small scales, states can be enumerated directly and draw conditions determined by structural features (e.g., the first player taking an endpoint or edge position can force a draw). The solution route is to compute small-scale DP to find periodic patterns and then extrapolate. When judging draws, pay attention to the termination rule 'when all objects are taken, it is a draw'. Common pitfalls include period start-point offset, failing to distinguish DP state differences caused by player turn alternation, and misjudging a draw under optimal play as a forced win for one side. For small n, use memoized game search to find the period: f(N) = ⌊N/p⌋ + g(N mod p) (where p is often a small number such as 7, and g is a table lookup); substitute large N to obtain the numerical result (e.g., N = 7q + r ⇒ q + g(r)). For draw determination, note the termination rule 'all taken means draw' and the structure where the first player taking an endpoint forces a draw.
applicability: Perfect-information take-number/placement games
Games where results exhibit modular periodicity with small period p (e.g., p = 7)
Small-scale state enumeration for draw condition analysis
Games with termination rule: 'when all objects are taken, it is a draw'
Games where the first player can force a draw by taking an endpoint or edge position

steps.step: Model the game state and define the DP/minimax recurrence
steps.detail: Define the state representation (e.g., remaining objects N, current player turn). Set up the minimax recurrence: a state is winning if there exists a move to a losing state for the opponent; losing if all moves lead to winning states for the opponent. Account for turn alternation explicitly in the state to avoid errors.

steps.step: Compute small-scale values via memoized search or DP
steps.detail: Calculate f(N) for small N (e.g., N = 0, 1, 2, ...) using memoized game search or bottom-up DP. Record the outcome (win/loss/draw) for each state. Pay attention to the base case: when all objects are taken (N = 0), the result is a draw per the termination rule.

steps.step: Identify periodicity in the sequence of outcomes
steps.detail: Inspect the computed sequence for periodic behavior. If a period p is detected (commonly a small number like 7), express the general solution as f(N) = ⌊N/p⌋ + g(N mod p), where g is a lookup table for the remainder. Verify the period start point to avoid offset errors.

steps.step: Extrapolate to large N using the periodic closed form
steps.detail: For large N, write N = p·q + r with 0 ≤ r < p. Compute the result as q + g(r). For example, if p = 7 and N = 7q + r, the value is q + g(r). Ensure the lookup table g is correctly indexed by the remainder r.

steps.step: Analyze draw conditions via structural features
steps.detail: When determining draws, check the termination rule: if all objects are taken, the game is a draw. Additionally, identify structural patterns such as the first player being able to force a draw by taking an endpoint or edge position. Do not misclassify an optimal-play draw as a forced win for either player.

template.name: Extremal Variable Count and Constrained ±1 Subsequence via Total Estimate and Explicit Construction
template.description: Given variable ranges and equality constraints on sums or sums of squares, determine the minimum number of variables; or, in a ±1 symbol sequence, determine the maximum guaranteed absolute value of a subsequence sum under the constraint that adjacent selected indices have bounded spacing. Unified technique: first use total-quantity estimation to give a bound (sum of squares strictly less than the number of variables; pair elements after grouping by fixed length), then prove the bound is attainable via an explicit sign-balanced construction. Common pitfalls: violating secondary constraints during construction (e.g., absolute total sum less than 1); miscalculating the upper bound on selectable elements per segment under spacing constraints; incorrect ceiling direction. For the 'between −1 and 1' case, by competition convention the interval is taken as open: the minimal-count-21 type (10 positive, 10 negative, plus one distinct value, using a √0.99-type construction). For ±1 sequences with spacing-constrained subsequences, the closed form is f(n) = ⌈(n+2)/4⌉, proved by a ++-- periodic construction and a lower bound from grouping every 4 elements; substitute the problem's n to obtain the numerical answer (e.g., 2022 → 506).
applicability: Problems asking for the minimum number of variables given ranges and sum / sum-of-squares equality constraints
Problems on ±1 sequences where a subsequence must respect a maximum gap between adjacent selected indices and one needs the maximum guaranteed absolute subsequence sum
Cases where the bound is established by total-quantity estimation on one side and explicit sign-balanced construction on the other
Open-interval 'between −1 and 1' competition problems requiring minimal variable count of the 21-variable type (10 positive, 10 negative, one distinct value)
±1 sequence problems with spacing constraints solvable by the f(n)=⌈(n+2)/4⌉ formula

steps.step: Apply total-quantity estimation to derive an upper/lower bound
steps.detail: Use aggregate constraints to bound the quantity of interest. For sum-of-squares problems, exploit the inequality that the sum of squares is strictly less than the number of variables (under the given range constraints). For ±1 sequence problems with spacing constraints, partition the sequence into fixed-length blocks (e.g., length 4) and count how many elements can be selected per block under the spacing rule, yielding a bound on the subsequence sum.

steps.step: Design an explicit sign-balanced construction to show the bound is attainable
steps.detail: Construct a concrete assignment that achieves the bound. For the open-interval 'between −1 and 1' minimal-variable case, use the 21-variable pattern: 10 variables set to a positive value, 10 to a negative value, and one distinct value (e.g., a √0.99-type construction) to satisfy the sum-of-squares equality while keeping the total sum's absolute value small. For the ±1 spacing-constrained subsequence problem, use the periodic ++-- pattern; within each block of 4, select elements according to the spacing rule to realize the claimed absolute sum.

steps.step: Verify all constraints and finalize the numerical answer
steps.detail: Check that the construction does not violate secondary constraints (e.g., ensure the absolute total sum is not forced below 1 when not required, and that the spacing constraint is respected). Confirm the ceiling direction in f(n)=⌈(n+2)/4⌉ is correct. Substitute the given n into the closed form to obtain the final value (e.g., for n=2022, f(2022)=⌈2024/4⌉=506).

template.name: Bounding via Locked Region and Per-Round Capacity
template.description: A two-player turn-based strategy for establishing a guaranteed score (or number of occupied cells). The first player secures a lower bound by locking onto a fixed-size target region (e.g., a small block or a monochromatic set of cells) and occupying it cell-by-cell, choosing a region far from the opponent's reach. The second player establishes an upper bound via capacity counting: upper bound = (maximum number of rounds) × (maximum cells the opponent can fill per round). When the lower and upper bounds coincide, the guaranteed value is determined. Critical details: account for the first-player's round advantage (turn-order parity); ensure the upper-bound argument covers the opponent's entire strategy space; correctly compute the per-round capacity. In non-attacking monochromatic configurations (e.g., a knight landing only on black squares), t rounds consume 2t cells of that color, so the guaranteed number equals (total cells of that color)/2 (e.g., 1200 black cells → 600).
applicability: Turn-based two-player games where players alternately occupy cells or claim resources.
Games where a player can lock a fixed target region to guarantee a minimum score.
Games where an opponent's per-round move capacity can be bounded to derive a global upper bound.
Scenarios involving monochromatic or non-attacking cell sets (e.g., knight moves restricted to one color class).
Problems where lower and upper bounds can be matched to pin down an exact guaranteed value.

steps.step: First player selects and locks a fixed target region
steps.detail: Choose a fixed-size region (e.g., a small square block or a monochromatic cell set) that is far from the opponent's reachable positions. Commit to occupying this region cell-by-cell throughout the game. This yields a lower bound equal to the size of the locked region (or the number of cells the first player can secure within it).

steps.step: First player accounts for turn-order advantage
steps.detail: Because the first player moves first, the number of rounds available to the first player may exceed that of the second player by one. Ensure this parity difference is reflected in the lower-bound calculation; ignoring it is a common error.

steps.step: Second player computes per-round capacity
steps.detail: Determine the maximum number of cells the second player can fill (or claim) in a single round. This capacity must be calculated correctly and must hold against all possible strategies of the first player.

steps.step: Second player derives the upper bound
steps.detail: Upper bound = (maximum number of rounds the second player can participate in) × (per-round capacity). The argument must cover the opponent's entire strategy space; otherwise the upper bound is invalid.

steps.step: Match bounds to obtain the guaranteed value
steps.detail: If the lower bound (from the locked region) equals the upper bound (from capacity counting), the common value is the guaranteed score/number of cells the first player can secure.

steps.step: Special case: monochromatic non-attacking sets
steps.detail: For configurations where pieces of one color do not attack each other (e.g., a knight always on black squares), each round t consumes 2t cells of that color. Hence the guaranteed number equals (total cells of that color)/2. Example calibration: 1200 black cells → guaranteed 600.

template.name: Binary Characterization of P-positions in Subtraction Games
template.description: In backward-induction game dynamic programming, the sets of N-positions (winning) and P-positions (losing, second-player win) can often be characterized using binary representations. Specifically, a position is a P-position (second-player win) if and only if all positions of 1s in its binary representation fall on odd-numbered bits, where the least significant bit is indexed as bit 0. Using this criterion, one can directly determine the game type and query the smallest number satisfying the condition over very large ranges without exhaustive DP. The solution route first handles the boundary segment where only +1 moves are available (the interval exceeding half the range), then induces the complete binary criterion; queries are answered by directly constructing numbers according to the criterion. Common pitfalls include confusion about the bit indexing origin (least significant bit is bit 0) and omitting boundary cases in the interval where two move types are available (positions below half the range).
applicability: Impartial combinatorial games solvable by backward-induction dynamic programming
Games where the P-position set admits a binary-pattern characterization
Scenarios requiring direct determination of game type or querying the minimum valid number over large ranges

steps.step: Identify the boundary segment where only +1 moves are possible
steps.detail: Determine the interval near the terminal state where the game rules restrict moves to +1 only (typically positions exceeding half of the maximum range). Analyze this boundary segment first to establish base cases for the induction.

steps.step: Induce the binary characterization of P-positions
steps.detail: From the boundary analysis, generalize the pattern: a state n is a P-position (losing for the player about to move, i.e., second-player win) if and only if in the binary representation of n, every bit equal to 1 occurs at an odd index, where the least significant bit (LSB) is defined as index 0. Formally, if n = Σ b_i · 2^i with b_i ∈ {0,1}, then n is a P-position ⇔ ∀i: b_i = 1 ⇒ i is odd.

steps.step: Classify any position using the binary criterion
steps.detail: To determine whether a given position n is an N-position or P-position, write n in binary and check the indices of all 1-bits. If all 1-bits are at odd positions (1, 3, 5, ...), it is a P-position; otherwise it is an N-position. This avoids computing the full DP table.

steps.step: Construct the smallest number satisfying a target condition
steps.detail: When querying for the smallest number that is a P-position (or satisfies a related condition), directly construct it by placing 1-bits only at odd indices (e.g., 2^1 + 2^3 + ... as needed), ensuring minimality by using the smallest available odd-indexed bits first.

steps.step: Handle boundary cases carefully
steps.detail: Pay special attention to the interval below half the range where two move types may be available; ensure boundary positions are not omitted. Double-check that bit indexing starts at 0 for the least significant bit to avoid off-by-one errors in the parity test.

template.name: Invariant Pairing and Mirror Strategy
template.description: A strategy where one player pairs objects according to an invariant (such as vector XOR summing to zero, pair sums being constant, or symmetric positions), then mirrors the opponent's choice each round to ensure a specific invariant (XOR sum, numerical difference, or rank) never becomes disadvantageous. The feasibility of pairing and handling of degenerate cases are determined by the underlying algebraic structure (linear space, constant sum). Key warnings: degenerate cases (empty set or self-pairing) can invalidate the strategy; mirror responses must be verified as legal under game rules; invariants must be maintained throughout the entire game, not just for a single step.
applicability: Games where objects can be paired such that each pair has XOR sum zero (in GF(2)^m) or constant sum
Games with symmetric positions allowing mirror responses
Scenarios where a global invariant (XOR sum, numerical difference) can be preserved through paired moves
Specific calibration: GF(2)^m card games where full set XOR sum is 0; numerical pair games with constant sum 51

steps.step: Identify the invariant that governs pairing
steps.detail: Determine whether the game admits pairing by XOR sum zero (in GF(2)^m), constant pair sum (e.g., each pair sums to 51), or symmetric positions. For GF(2)^m cards, the full set XOR sum must be 0. For numerical pairs, check if pairs can be formed as (50,1), (49,2), ... each summing to 51.

steps.step: Construct the pairing scheme
steps.detail: For GF(2)^m: pair each vector x with x⊕c where c is a constant (for second player, c is the first player's move). For numerical pairs with constant sum S: pair (a, S-a). For symmetric positions: pair each position with its symmetric counterpart. Ensure no object pairs with itself unless it is a fixed point that preserves the invariant.

steps.step: Handle degenerate cases
steps.detail: Check for empty set or self-pairing scenarios. In GF(2)^m card game, the empty card (zero vector) is the unique losing first move for the first player when full XOR sum is 0. If an object must pair with itself, verify whether the invariant still holds or if the strategy fails.

steps.step: Execute mirror response
steps.detail: When opponent selects an object from a pair, immediately select the paired object. Verify this move is legal under game rules. For GF(2)^m: if opponent picks x, pick x⊕c. For constant sum pairs: if opponent picks a, pick S-a. For symmetry: if opponent picks position p, pick symmetric position p'.

steps.step: Verify invariant preservation throughout
steps.detail: Confirm after each round that the invariant (XOR sum, numerical difference of type 3k, or rank) remains non-disadvantageous. Use backward induction for numerical pair games to ensure bilateral optimality. Do not assume single-step preservation guarantees game-long preservation.

template.name: Parity Invariants and Collision Equivalence for Grid Processes
template.description: A unified strategy for worst-case analysis of propagation and movement processes on a grid. For infection spread, the method uses a parity invariant on local blocks: a deadlock configuration is one where every 2×2 block contains an even number of infected cells (0, 2, or 4), which forces the total infection count to remain unchanged under the flip rule. The maximal size of such a deadlock set is n²/4 + n/2 (constructed via periodic patterns plus boundary row/column padding), so the minimum guaranteed infection threshold is k = n²/4 + n/2 + 1. For ant collisions, the method applies the equivalence model where a collision is treated as two ants passing through each other and exchanging identities; this decomposes each ant's path into at most two segments (one horizontal, one vertical), yielding a latest departure time of 1.5N − 1, achieved by a head-on collision construction at the midline. Common pitfalls include assuming the flip rule changes total infection count, missing configurations where paths exceed two segments after turning, and miscalculating half-integer coordinate meeting points.
applicability: Infection spread processes on an n×n grid with local flip rules
Ant collision problems on an N×N board with unit-speed motion
Worst-case upper bound analysis via parity invariants
Problems where collisions can be modeled as identity exchange and straight-line continuation

steps.step: Identify the local parity invariant for infection problems
steps.detail: Define the infection count modulo 2 within every 2×2 local block. A configuration is a deadlock if and only if every 2×2 block has infection count ∈ {0, 2, 4}. Under the flip rule, such blocks can only be flipped as a whole, leaving the total infection count unchanged.

steps.step: Construct the maximal deadlock configuration
steps.detail: Build a periodic pattern where all 2×2 blocks have even infection counts, then pad boundary rows/columns to maximize size. The maximal deadlock set size is n²/4 + n/2. Therefore, if the initial infected set has size k ≥ n²/4 + n/2 + 1, the system cannot be deadlocked and must spread further.

steps.step: Calibrate the infection bound with small n
steps.detail: Verify the formula n²/4 + n/2 by explicit simulation for n = 2, 3, 4 to ensure the periodic construction and boundary padding produce the claimed maximal deadlock sizes.

steps.step: Apply collision equivalence for ant problems
steps.detail: Replace every physical collision (where two ants meet and reverse direction) with a virtual event where the ants pass through each other but swap identities. This preserves the set of occupied positions over time and simplifies path tracking.

steps.step: Decompose ant paths into at most two segments
steps.detail: Under the equivalence model, each ant moves in a straight line until a virtual crossing, after which it continues in the orthogonal direction. Thus each ant's trajectory consists of at most one horizontal segment and one vertical segment.

steps.step: Compute the latest departure time
steps.detail: The longest possible path under the two-segment decomposition is achieved when two ants start at opposite edges and collide at the midline, causing one ant to traverse a full horizontal segment plus half a vertical segment (or vice versa). This gives a latest departure time of 1.5N − 1. A construction with two ants colliding head-on at the midline attains this bound.

template.name: Worst-case optimal query determination and maximal histogram frequency covering
template.description: This strategy addresses two classes of worst-case optimal quantity problems. First, determining the minimum query set required to uniquely identify a hidden structure under any possible response: construct an explicit query scheme and prove a lower bound by exhibiting two configurations indistinguishable under two responses. Second, placing large square tiles on a board to maximize the highest frequency in the coverage-count histogram: first tile the main region with non-overlapping tiles (coverage value 1), then incrementally add tiles along boundary strips to balance new coverage against overlap, with corner adjustments. Caveats include redundancy and overlap in query schemes, double-counting of boundary corner regions, and the exclusion of empty positions with coverage value zero from histogram statistics.
applicability: Problems requiring the minimum number of queries to uniquely determine a hidden structure under worst-case responses
Problems on a grid/board where large square tiles are placed to maximize the most frequent coverage count in the histogram
Scenarios where the main region can be fully covered by non-overlapping tiles and boundary strips require incremental balancing of new coverage versus overlap

steps.step: Construct the query scheme for hidden structure determination
steps.detail: Query the entire layer fully, then supplement with queries on odd-numbered columns of adjacent faces. For the calibrated 324 + 162 = 486 type, this yields 486 total queries. Ensure the scheme avoids redundancy and unnecessary overlap.

steps.step: Prove the query lower bound via indistinguishable configurations
steps.detail: Exhibit two distinct configurations that produce identical responses to any query in the candidate set, thereby showing that fewer queries cannot uniquely determine the hidden structure. This is an information-theoretic style 'cannot distinguish two configurations' argument.

steps.step: Tile the main region for the histogram covering problem
steps.detail: Place ⌊n/k⌋² non-overlapping large square tiles to fully cover the main region, giving every cell in that region coverage value 1. Here n is the board dimension and k is the tile side length parameter.

steps.step: Incrementally add tiles along boundary strips
steps.detail: Along two boundary edges, add tiles incrementally to balance the gain in newly covered cells against the cost of overlapping existing coverage. Adjust corner regions carefully to avoid double-counting.

steps.step: Compute the histogram and exclude zero-coverage cells
steps.detail: Form the histogram of coverage counts across all cells. Remember that empty positions with coverage value 0 are not counted in the statistics. The objective is to maximize the highest frequency (mode) in this histogram.

template.name: Periodic Coloring and Capacity Lower Bound for Board Covering
template.description: Partition the board into color classes using periodic colorings (e.g., by (i+j) mod k or by parity classes of coordinates), count the number of squares in each class, and compute the coverage capacity of each piece type (L-shaped, corner-removed rectangular blocks, etc.) on these color classes to derive a lower bound on the number of pieces required or on the number of covering configurations; then explicitly construct a scheme achieving the lower bound. The coloring must match the piece shape (e.g., diagonal squares same color, arms and corner different colors); the lower bound is usually given by the scarcest color class. Common pitfalls: mismatch between coloring pattern and piece coverage capacity yielding a loose lower bound; forgetting rotations and reflections of pieces; misclassifying boundary squares. Step-by-step closure: first write the area equation (2d + 4s = total area); minimizing d is equivalent to maximizing s. Under the (i+j) mod 3 three-coloring, the color distribution of an S-shaped block is (0,2,2) or (2,1,1); color counts give a lower bound on d. Achieve equality via 2×3 block partition plus boundary completion. Anti-pattern (disprove first, then assert impossibility): if a piece's color ratio under the coloring is not unique (e.g., a 3-square L-tromino can cover either 2 black + 1 white or 1 black + 2 white), then the fact that the total number of target squares is not divisible by 3 does NOT constitute a proof of impossibility. Before declaring impossibility, actually construct on small boards such as 3×3 or 5×5; if small-scale construction succeeds, the argument is flawed. Lower-bound selection: do not use the crude bound 'target squares ÷ maximum coverage per piece'—it is usually unattainable and below the true value. Instead, find a scarce subclass that any single piece can cover at most one square of (typically the class of squares with coordinates (odd, odd)); the number of squares in that subclass is the tight lower bound (on an n×n alternating black-corner board, black squares split into ⌈n/2⌉² and ⌊n/2⌋² classes; take the ⌈n/2⌉² class as the tight lower bound), then give an explicit tiling achieving it. Construction and lower bound must meet: if the construction cannot reach the crude bound, take the construction value as the answer and explain that the crude bound is unreachable due to boundary/parity obstruction.
applicability: Board covering/tiling problems with L-shaped trominoes, tetrominoes, corner-removed blocks, dominoes, and similar pieces
Deriving tight lower bounds via color-class scarcity rather than crude area division
Proving impossibility or optimality by matching explicit constructions to coloring lower bounds
Problems where piece color ratios are non-unique and small-board calibration is required before asserting impossibility

steps.step: Choose a periodic coloring matched to the piece shape
steps.detail: Use colorings such as (i+j) mod k or coordinate parity classes so that the piece's squares have a fixed or limited color pattern (e.g., diagonal squares same color, arms and corner different colors). Ensure boundary squares are classified correctly.

steps.step: Count squares per color class
steps.detail: Compute the exact number of board squares in each color class, including boundary effects. On an n×n alternating black-corner board, black squares split into ⌈n/2⌉² and ⌊n/2⌋² classes.

steps.step: Compute piece coverage capacity per color class
steps.detail: For each piece type (allowing all rotations and reflections), determine how many squares of each color class one piece can cover. For example, under (i+j) mod 3 three-coloring, an S-shaped block has color distribution (0,2,2) or (2,1,1). If a piece's color ratio is not unique (e.g., L-tromino can cover 2 black + 1 white or 1 black + 2 white), divisibility by the piece size alone does not prove impossibility.

steps.step: Derive the tight lower bound from the scarcest class
steps.detail: Avoid the crude bound 'target squares ÷ maximum coverage per piece'. Instead identify a scarce subclass that any single piece can cover at most one square of (typically the (odd, odd) coordinate class). The tight lower bound is the size of that subclass (e.g., ⌈n/2⌉² on an n×n alternating black-corner board). Write area equations when relevant, e.g., 2d + 4s = total area, where minimizing d is equivalent to maximizing s.

steps.step: Calibrate on small boards before asserting impossibility
steps.detail: If the coloring argument suggests impossibility, first attempt explicit construction on small boards such as 3×3 or 5×5. If a small-scale construction exists, the impossibility argument is invalid.

steps.step: Construct an explicit tiling achieving the lower bound
steps.detail: Give a concrete covering that meets the lower bound, for example by 2×3 block partition plus boundary completion. If the construction cannot reach the crude bound, take the construction value as the answer and state that the crude bound is unreachable due to boundary or parity obstruction.

template.name: Symmetry-Parameterized Orbit Counting on Lattices and 3D Grids
template.description: When counting on symmetric grids or 3D lattices, first parameterize objects by symmetry. Regular hexagons are determined by side length and center position (two center types: lattice points and cell centers). 3D cells are partitioned into orbit classes by coordinate equality patterns (all equal, exactly two equal, all distinct) and by the parity of coordinate permutations. Counting then reduces to summing over parameters and orbit representatives. For triangular grids, carefully determine the valid ranges for both center types. For 3D problems, stratify color classes by 'coordinate equality pattern + permutation parity'. Common pitfalls include missing same-type objects in special rotation directions (e.g., slanted regular hexagons), double-counting orbit classes, and incorrectly bounding parameter ranges (e.g., maximum side length).
applicability: Counting regular hexagons on triangular grids including all rotation orientations
Counting color/orbit classes on 3D n×n×n grids under coordinate permutation symmetry
Problems where global constraints couple colors across three directional slices (colors must lie at intersections of slices, not independently assigned per cell)
Verification of polynomial/closed-form answers by brute-force enumeration at small n before extrapolation

steps.step: Parameterize hexagons on triangular grid
steps.detail: Identify regular hexagons by side length s and center type. There are two center classes: centers at lattice points and centers at cell centers (grid hexagon centers). For each center type, determine the valid range of s given the board boundary. Sum over all valid (center, s) pairs. Do not count only axis-aligned hexagons; include slanted orientations.

steps.step: Sum hexagon counts via cubic sum identity
steps.detail: The total count of regular hexagons (all orientations) on a triangular grid of size n involves summing s³ over side lengths. Use the identity Σ s³ = (n(n+1)/2)² (the square triangular number) to close the sum. Ensure the upper limit of s matches the board geometry.

steps.step: Classify 3D cells by coordinate equality pattern
steps.detail: For an n×n×n grid with coordinates (x,y,z), partition cells into three strata: (1) all equal: x=y=z, contributing n cells; (2) exactly two equal: e.g., x=y≠z, x=z≠y, y=z≠x, contributing 3·C(n,2) cells; (3) all distinct: x,y,z all different.

steps.step: Subdivide all-distinct class by permutation parity
steps.detail: For cells with all distinct coordinates, further split by the parity of the permutation ordering the coordinates. This yields two orbit classes under coordinate permutations, contributing 2·C(n,3) cells in total.

steps.step: Handle coupled color constraints across three directional slices
steps.detail: When the problem imposes that the color multisets of three directional slices are identical, this is a global constraint: colors can only be placed at the intersections of the three slice families and are mutually coupled. Do NOT treat each cell as independently colorable.

steps.step: Calibrate with small n before final extrapolation
steps.detail: Use small n (e.g., n=2,3) for brute-force enumeration to verify the derived formula. If the enumerated value disagrees with the proposed closed form (e.g., an n³-type power answer), the modeling is incorrect. Only after calibration should the formula be evaluated at the problem's actual scale. Never report the small-n calibration value as the final answer.

template.name: Minimum Maximal Matching Set in Complete Graphs with Conflict-Erase Guarantees
template.description: Abstract the real-world scheduling problem into a graph problem: the tournament schedule corresponds to a minimum-cardinality maximal set of edge-disjoint perfect matchings (1-factorizations) in a complete graph; the erase constraint corresponds to a covering guarantee on a conflict graph where at each step the vertex of highest degree is greedily selected and its conflicting neighbors are removed. Key conclusions: the size of the minimum maximal matching set in a complete graph takes the value 'half-pairs' or 'half-pairs plus one' depending on the parity of the vertex count; the presence of an odd-cycle structure in the conflict graph tightens the greedy guarantee. Upper bound uses the sufficient condition that the remaining graph has no perfect matching (it splits into two odd components); lower bound uses explicit 1-factorization construction; greedy selection proceeds by degree from large to small. Common pitfalls: parity of vertex count causes formula boundary errors; omitting the correspondence between 'each pair plays at most once' and edge-disjoint matchings; conflicts only occur between two objects whose pairings are opposite numbers. Final calibration: for K_{2n}, the minimum maximal matching set takes n+1 when n is even and n when n is odd (n=20→21); construction makes the complement of the union split into two odd components, with small cases K₄→3, K₆→3, K₈→5 for calibration; what is sought is 'the maximum number of rounds such that the schedule may terminate' = the n+1 type, not the full tournament round count 2n−1. Conflict-graph erase guarantee: greedily pick numbers by degree and delete conflicting neighbors; the odd-cycle structure ensures at most 2 points per every three pairs.
applicability: Problems abstractable to edge-disjoint perfect matchings (1-factors) in complete graphs K_{2n}
Scheduling problems where each pair meets at most once and the schedule may terminate early
Erase/removal constraints modeled by a conflict graph where conflicts occur only between opposite-numbered pairings
Deriving upper bounds via sufficient conditions for absence of perfect matching (splitting into two odd components)
Deriving lower bounds via explicit 1-factorization constructions
Greedy strategies ordered by degree on conflict graphs, especially those containing odd cycles

steps.step: Model the schedule as a graph problem
steps.detail: Map teams/players to vertices and matches to edges. A round in which every team plays exactly once corresponds to a perfect matching (1-factor). The requirement that each pair plays at most once translates to edge-disjoint matchings. The problem of the maximum number of rounds after which the schedule may become impossible to continue corresponds to finding a minimum-cardinality maximal set of edge-disjoint perfect matchings in K_{2n}.

steps.step: Apply the parity-dependent closed form for K_{2n}
steps.detail: For the complete graph K_{2n}, the size of the minimum maximal matching set depends on the parity of n: if n is even, the value is n+1; if n is odd, the value is n. Calibration: n=20 (even) gives 21. Small-case verification: K₄ (n=2) gives 3, K₆ (n=3) gives 3, K₈ (n=4) gives 5. Note that this is not the full 1-factorization count 2n−1; it is the 'maximum rounds such that the schedule may terminate' of the n+1 type.

steps.step: Establish the upper bound via odd-component splitting
steps.detail: To prove an upper bound, construct the union of the chosen matchings such that its complement (the remaining graph) has no perfect matching. A sufficient condition used here is that the remaining graph splits into two odd components, which precludes a perfect matching and forces maximality of the chosen set.

steps.step: Establish the lower bound via 1-factorization construction
steps.detail: To prove a lower bound, explicitly construct edge-disjoint perfect matchings using a 1-factorization of K_{2n}, showing that no smaller maximal set can exist below the parity-dependent threshold.

steps.step: Model the erase constraint with a conflict graph and apply greedy selection
steps.detail: When an erase/remove constraint is present, build a conflict graph where vertices represent candidate pairings and edges represent conflicts. Conflicts only occur between two objects whose pairings are opposite numbers. The covering guarantee is achieved by the greedy rule: at each step, select the vertex with the largest degree, then delete it and all its conflicting neighbors.

steps.step: Account for the odd-cycle tightening in the conflict graph
steps.detail: If the conflict graph contains an odd cycle, the greedy guarantee tightens: for every three pairs involved in the odd-cycle structure, at most 2 points (selections) can be obtained. This must be incorporated into the covering bound.

template.name: Minimum Lines for Bichromatic Point Separation
template.description: Given a set of red and blue marked points in the plane, the problem is to partition the plane into regions using straight lines that do not pass through any marked point, such that each region contains points of only one color. For any red-blue point configuration, the minimum number of lines required equals the number of points in the smaller color class, i.e., min(|red|, |blue|). The upper bound is established by a sweep construction: project all points onto a direction in general position, sort them along that direction, and draw a line between every adjacent pair of points with different colors. The lower bound is established by a narrow-strip alternating configuration where red and blue points strictly alternate, forcing a distinct line for each color change. A common pitfall is allowing a line to pass through a marked point, or assuming without complete proof that 'no region contains both colors' is equivalent to 'every adjacent opposite-colored pair is separated'. When coarse region-counting arguments conflict with the alternating-strip construction, the lower bound given by the alternating construction should be trusted.
applicability: Any finite configuration of red and blue marked points in the plane
Separating lines must not pass through any marked point
Each resulting region must contain points of at most one color
The exact minimum number of lines is min(|red|, |blue|)

steps.step: State the target quantity
steps.detail: The minimum number of straight lines needed to separate any red-blue point configuration in the plane is min(|red|, |blue|), where |red| and |blue| denote the numbers of red and blue points respectively.

steps.step: Upper bound: choose a projection direction
steps.detail: Select a direction (e.g., an angle θ) such that the orthogonal projections of all marked points onto a line with that direction are pairwise distinct. This is always possible because there are only finitely many forbidden directions determined by pairs of points.

steps.step: Upper bound: sort and scan
steps.detail: Sort the points by their projected coordinates along the chosen direction. Scan the sorted sequence and, whenever two adjacent points have different colors, draw a straight line perpendicular to the projection direction that separates these two points. Ensure no line passes through any marked point by placing it strictly between the two projections.

steps.step: Upper bound: count the lines
steps.detail: The number of lines drawn is at most the number of color changes in the sorted sequence, which cannot exceed the number of points in the smaller color class. Hence the number of lines is ≤ min(|red|, |blue|).

steps.step: Lower bound: construct an alternating narrow-strip configuration
steps.detail: Arrange the points inside a very narrow strip such that their colors strictly alternate along the strip (e.g., R, B, R, B, ...). Because the strip is narrow, any line that separates two consecutive points of different colors must cut across the strip, and each such color transition requires a distinct line.

steps.step: Lower bound: count forced lines
steps.detail: In the alternating configuration, if the smaller color class has k points, there are at least k color transitions that must be separated, requiring at least k distinct lines. Therefore the minimum number of lines is ≥ min(|red|, |blue|).

steps.step: Combine bounds and conclude
steps.detail: Since the upper bound and lower bound both equal min(|red|, |blue|), the exact minimum number of lines for any red-blue point configuration is min(|red|, |blue|).

steps.step: Verify implementation constraints
steps.detail: Check that no constructed line passes through a marked point. Also verify that the equivalence between 'no region contains both colors' and 'every adjacent opposite-colored pair in the projection order is separated' is rigorously justified; do not leave this equivalence as an unproved assertion.

template.name: Constrained Domino Covering via Row-Column Selection and Alternating Cycle Breaking
template.description: This strategy addresses constrained domino placement on a chessboard where, within each small square group, the uncovered cells satisfy a same-row/same-column condition. The set of uncovered cells corresponds to a row-column selection structure: choosing several rows and several columns whose intersection points are exactly the uncovered cells. The counting problem is thereby reduced to combinatorial binomial coefficients. When marked cells are used to enforce a unique covering, the role of the marks is to destroy all flippable alternating cycles; the required number of marks is of the same order as the board side length. The solution route translates constraints into shape characteristics of the uncovered-cell set; uniqueness arguments revolve around flippable covering cycles; and small-scale verification cross-validates the general formula. Common pitfalls include omitting the equivalence-direction derivation between constraints and the diagonal-uncovered pattern, asserting uniqueness without fully destroying flippable cycles, and failing to investigate discrepancies between small-scale enumeration and the formula. Final step summary: uncovered cells = intersection structure of selected k rows × k columns ⇒ counting is of the form C(2k,k)² (square of a binomial coefficient); calibrated using brute-force values for k=1,2 as 4 and 36; the answer must be reported as the combinatorial expression or its numerical value, and linear forms such as 2(k+1) are forbidden.
applicability: Constrained domino covering problems on a chessboard where uncovered cells in each small square group satisfy same-row/same-column conditions
Problems whose uncovered-cell set can be represented as the intersection of selected rows and selected columns
Counting problems reducible to squared binomial-coefficient forms C(2k,k)²
Uniqueness-enforcement problems where marked cells are used to break flippable alternating cycles
Cases requiring small-scale calibration (e.g., k=1,2) to validate general combinatorial formulas

steps.step: Translate constraints into the shape characteristic of the uncovered-cell set
steps.detail: Interpret the constraint (within each small square group, uncovered cells lie in the same row or same column) as a structural condition on the uncovered cells. Establish the equivalence direction carefully: the uncovered-cell set must correspond to a row-column selection structure, i.e., the intersection of some chosen rows and some chosen columns. Do not omit the derivation showing that this is equivalent to the 'diagonal uncovered' pattern under the given constraints.

steps.step: Model the uncovered cells as a k×k row-column intersection
steps.detail: Let the uncovered cells be exactly the intersection points of k selected rows and k selected columns. This yields a k×k grid of uncovered cells at those intersections. Under this structure, the counting of valid coverings reduces to choosing the rows and columns, leading to a combinatorial closed form.

steps.step: Derive the combinatorial counting formula
steps.detail: With the row-column selection model, the number of valid configurations is of the form C(2k,k)², i.e., the square of the binomial coefficient choosing k from 2k. Preserve this exact parameterized closed form; do not replace it with a linear expression.

steps.step: Calibrate the formula with small-scale brute-force values
steps.detail: Verify the formula against explicit enumeration for small k: for k=1, the brute-force count is 4; for k=2, the brute-force count is 36. If the general formula does not match these calibration values, investigate the discrepancy rather than ignoring it.

steps.step: Handle uniqueness enforcement via marked cells and alternating cycle breaking
steps.detail: When unique covering is required, introduce marked cells to force the covering. The function of the marks is to destroy all flippable alternating cycles (cycles in the covered region that can be flipped to produce another valid covering). The number of marks required is of the same order as the board side length. Do not claim uniqueness unless all flippable alternating cycles have been fully destroyed.

steps.step: Report the final answer in the correct form
steps.detail: Present the answer as the combinatorial expression C(2k,k)² or its evaluated numerical value. Linear forms such as 2(k+1) are explicitly forbidden.

template.name: Binary Invariant in Merge-Erase Games
template.description: In numerical games involving merging or erasing operations, the invariant is often hidden in the binary representation of the quantities. For merging processes where each step takes equal amounts from two piles to form a new pile, if the total is not a power of two, at least two non-empty piles remain, corresponding to a sum-of-powers decomposition. In erasing/merasing games, the number of remaining items at termination equals the number of 1s in the binary representation of the initial total (conserved under optimal play). The solution route is: first analyze the binary characteristics of the initial quantity (number of 1s, whether it is a power of two); then prove each operation preserves this characteristic. Common pitfalls: merging operations require taking equal amounts from two piles; when not fully merging, the remaining structure differs. The proof that 'the number of 1s in the binary sum' and 'the number of remaining items' is conserved must cover both sides of optimal play. For the specific game of N copies of 1 where two numbers are erased and their sum is written: the guaranteed value equals popcount(N) (the number of 1s in binary, e.g., N=1997→11111001101→8). One strategy maintains that all numbers have pairwise disjoint binary bits; the other pairs and merges according to power-of-two decomposition. First compute popcount to determine the candidate, then complete the strategy loop for both sides.
applicability: Numerical games with merging or erasing operations where quantities are combined or replaced
Games where each step takes equal amounts from two piles to merge into a new pile
Termination-state analysis for erase-two-numbers-write-sum type games
Initial total N composed of N copies of 1
Optimal play scenarios where both players' strategies must be accounted for

steps.step: Analyze binary characteristics of the initial total
steps.detail: Compute the binary representation of the initial total quantity. Record the number of 1s (popcount) and check whether the total is a power of two. For example, if N = 1997, its binary is 11111001101, giving popcount(1997) = 8.

steps.step: Identify the invariant
steps.detail: For merging processes: if the total is not a power of two, at least two non-empty piles must remain, corresponding to a decomposition into a sum of powers of two. For erasing/merging games: the number of remaining items at termination equals popcount(initial total). This quantity is conserved under optimal play.

steps.detail: Show that each allowed operation (erasing two numbers and writing their sum, or merging equal amounts from two piles) does not change the number of 1s in the binary representation of the multiset of values when viewed as a sum of distinct powers of two. template.name: Row-Column Counting Duality and Matrix Poset Pigeonhole
template.description: A reusable strategy for extremal counting problems on binary matrices (or equivalent set systems). One class of problems encodes constraints as row-count/column-count pairs, using uniqueness of the pairing and degree-sequence feasibility conditions (Gale–Ryser type dual inequalities) to derive linear constraints, then tightens them to exact extremal values and proves attainability via explicit construction. The other class arranges objects into a matrix and uses poset chains/antichains together with the pigeonhole principle to prove that a crossing structure must appear once a critical threshold (on the order of the product of row and column dimensions plus one) is exceeded. Common pitfalls include confusing 'there exist two rows each with m entries' with 'every row has exactly m entries', omitting the monotone direction (ascending/descending) of the poset which invalidates the pigeonhole argument, and reversing the direction of the dual inequalities. A key calibration: 'two rows of degree m ⇒ their column-sum sets are disjoint ⇒ 2m ≤ n' is only the first constraint; one must further apply compressed-matrix inequalities of the form a·n_a ≤ n to tighten to an extremum on the order of m = n/2 − 4 and provide an explicit construction (remaining rows traverse the remaining degree values). For a two-interval family with total count t², the connectivity critical value is t(t−1)+1; the answer is the product plus one, not t itself.

steps.step: Tighten with compressed-matrix bounds

template.name: Potential Function and Frontier Width Threshold for Density Lower Bounds
template.description: For turn-based games on a grid where one party adds increments to a local neighborhood each round and the other party imposes a global bounded reduction each round, use a potential function defined as the ratio of net increment to affected area to prove a guaranteed density lower bound. For diffusion-type growth problems, classify sparsity using the expansion frontier width: if the frontier maintains two-dimensional expansion (width reaching a certain proportion of the board side length), growth is quadratic; otherwise it is confined to a one-dimensional strip (linear growth). The potential function is taken as (increment this round − opponent's reduction this round). The sparse threshold comes from converting the minimum width required to maintain a two-dimensional frontier into board side length. Common pitfalls: mistaking the per-round upper bound for a total upper bound; miscalculating boundary neighborhood effects (corner cells, edge cells); and confusing the conversion relation between frontier width and round number. The sparse threshold equals the critical initial quantity required to maintain a two-dimensional frontier, of the form s = (side length)² − (⌊side length/2⌋ + 1)² (e.g., for side length 75: 75² − 38² = 4181). If s is below this threshold, growth is confined to a one-dimensional strip (O(n)); if s reaches this threshold, Ω(n²) growth can be maintained. The requested 'minimum non-sparse s' is the threshold itself, not the threshold minus one.

steps.detail: Set the potential function as the ratio of net increment to affected area. Specifically, potential = (increment this round − opponent's reduction this round) / (affected area). Use this to argue for a guaranteed density lower bound.

steps.detail: Measure the expansion frontier width. If the frontier maintains two-dimensional expansion with width reaching a certain proportion of the board side length, growth is quadratic. If the frontier is too narrow, growth is confined to a one-dimensional strip and is at most linear.

steps.step: Compute the sparse threshold
steps.detail: The sparse threshold is the critical initial quantity needed to maintain a two-dimensional frontier. It follows the closed form s = L² − (⌊L/2⌋ + 1)², where L is the board side length. For example, when L = 75: s = 75² − 38² = 5625 − 1444 = 4181.

steps.step: Determine growth regime
steps.detail: If the initial quantity s is below the threshold, growth is limited to a one-dimensional strip (O(n)). If s reaches or exceeds the threshold, Ω(n²) growth can be maintained.

steps.step: Identify the minimum non-sparse s
steps.detail: The requested 'minimum non-sparse s' is exactly the threshold value itself, not the threshold minus one.

steps.detail: Do not mistake the per-round upper bound for a total upper bound. Carefully compute boundary neighborhood effects for corner cells and edge cells. Maintain the correct conversion relation between frontier width and round number.

template.name: Recursive Counting for Independent Sets and Monotone Paths on Grids
template.description: When counting strictly increasing numerical sequences or independent sets on paths and chessboards, use recurrence relations. For independent sets on a path graph, the counting polynomial satisfies a first-order linear recurrence via binary choice at each node (exclude current node / include current node; if included, the predecessor must be excluded). For chessboard path counting, construct a snake-like or spiral numbering so that each cell has at most one incoming edge and one outgoing edge, reducing the problem to counting sources (local minima) in a directed acyclic graph (DAG). The construction aims to make the number of local-minimum starting points reach the theoretical lower bound. Common pitfalls: omitting the predecessor-exclusion constraint in the independent-set recurrence; missing row/column parity conditions for local minima; and neglecting that boundary cells have fewer neighbors than interior cells.
applicability: Counting independent sets on path graphs via first-order linear recurrence with explicit initial conditions (empty graph, single vertex).
Counting monotone/increasing paths on n×n boards by snake-like or spiral numbering that converts the board into a DAG with at most one incoming and one outgoing edge per cell.
Establishing lower bounds by counting DAG sources (local minima), where optimal starting-point count takes the form ⌈n/2⌉² + ⌊n/2⌋² (e.g., for n=157: 78² + 77² = 12013).

steps.step: Set up the independent-set recurrence on a path
steps.detail: Let I_k denote the number of independent sets on the first k nodes of a path. By binary choice at node k: (1) do not select node k → I_{k-1} ways; (2) select node k → predecessor k−1 cannot be selected, giving I_{k-2} ways. Hence I_k = I_{k-1} + I_{k-2}. State initial conditions explicitly: I_0 = 1 (empty graph), I_1 = 2 (either select the single vertex or not). For weighted/independent-set polynomials, attach a weight variable x for each selected node, yielding P_k = P_{k-1} + x·P_{k-2} with P_0 = 1, P_1 = 1 + x.

steps.step: Construct snake-like or spiral numbering on the chessboard
steps.detail: Assign numbers to the n×n grid cells in a snake-like (row-wise alternating direction) or spiral order so that any allowed path step moves from a smaller number to a larger number. This ensures each cell has at most one incoming edge and one outgoing edge in the induced directed graph, making it a DAG.

steps.step: Identify local-minimum sources via parity conditions
steps.detail: In the constructed DAG, a cell can be a path starting point only if it is a local minimum under the numbering. For snake-like fill on a square board, the good path starting points correspond to cells whose row and column indices are both even (or both odd, depending on orientation). Boundary cells have fewer neighbors than interior cells, so verify the local-minimum condition carefully at edges and corners.

steps.step: Count sources to obtain the lower bound
steps.detail: Count the number of local-minimum cells. For an n×n board under the snake/spiral construction, the optimal count of starting points equals ⌈n/2⌉² + ⌊n/2⌋². For example, when n=157, this gives 78² + 77² = 6084 + 5929 = 12013. This source count proves the lower bound for the number of necessary path starting points.

template.name: Translation-invariant total order parity counting via coprime slope parametrization
template.description: A bijection with translation-order-preserving property is equivalent to a translation-invariant total order. Such an order is determined by a positive cone and has the form 'stratified by a linear functional + tie-breaking rule within each layer'. Its rank function can be written as two parts: 'layer count + intra-layer offset'. Based on this, one performs exact parity statistics of ranks over a target rectangular region, and traverses the feasible parameter family (coprime slopes and tie-breaking rules) to find extremal values. Common pitfalls include: reversing the equivalence direction between 'order-preserving bijection' and 'translation-invariant total order'; different intra-layer tie-breaking rules (smaller x first vs. smaller y first) yield different counts; and the half-open interval boundaries of the target region. Final summary: order = linear functional stratification + intra-layer tie-breaking direction; the parity count N varies with coprime parameters (p,q) and tie-breaking direction within [N_min, N_max], where the two endpoints are attained by the two tie-breaking rules under extreme slopes of type (1,q); when the required answer is a product or combination of endpoints, one must traverse the parameter family to obtain both endpoints, and it is forbidden to compute only one group.

template.name: LZ Dictionary Encoding with Fixed-Length Codewords
template.description: LZ encoding decomposes a message into a phrase sequence of the form "already-appeared phrase + new character". Each phrase is represented as a (dictionary index, character) pair, and the dictionary is dynamically expanded during encoding. The index and character are then concatenated into an encoded bit string according to a given fixed-length character mapping. The greedy matching strategy selects the longest already-appeared prefix at each step. Each codeword consists of the binary representation of the index concatenated with the binary representation of the character. Note that the number of bits for the index may change as the dictionary size grows. Common pitfalls include: greedy matching being too long so that the next phrase cannot be matched; inconsistent starting index (0 vs 1); and incorrect fixed-length bit-width conventions. For the required output format, each phrase must produce a concatenated bit string of "index binary (fixed 3 bits) + character code (3 bits)", with indices starting from 0. Providing only the phrase decomposition earns partial credit; the complete bit string is the full answer.

steps.step: Initialize the dictionary and parse the message greedily
steps.detail: Start with an empty or predefined dictionary. Scan the message from left to right, and at each position greedily match the longest prefix that already appears in the dictionary. The phrase is then this matched prefix plus the next new character. The dictionary is dynamically expanded as new phrases are identified.

steps.step: Represent each phrase as an (index, character) pair
steps.detail: For each decomposed phrase, record it as a pair (dictionary index, character), where the index points to the already-appeared prefix in the dictionary and the character is the new character that extends it.

steps.step: Convert each pair into a fixed-length binary codeword

steps.step: Assemble the final output bit string
